questions.q: What makes a script "reusable" in the sense this lesson means?
options: Inputs like database names or thresholds are declared as variables at the top instead of hardcoded into the query body
It uses as many joins as possible
It's written entirely in one line
It only ever runs against AdventureWorks
questions.explain: Parameterizing inputs means the exact same script runs unedited against any database or server.

questions.q: Why does a @DryRun flag default to 1 instead of 0?
options: So the script only prints what it would do by default, and someone has to deliberately flip it to run for real
Because 0 is not a valid bit value in SQL Server
Because SQL Server requires all flags to default to 1
It doesn't matter which value it defaults to
questions.explain: Defaulting to safe (print-only) means a mistake or an accidental run can't cause damage — the dangerous branch requires a deliberate change.

questions.q: Which kind of script generally does NOT need a @DryRun guard?
options: A read-only SELECT against a DMV or catalog view
A script that runs KILL on a session
A script that disables a SQL Server Agent job
A script that deletes rows from a table
questions.explain: SELECT queries against DMVs and catalog views are always safe to run — they can't block or corrupt anything. Guards are for anything that writes.

questions.q: What does the header convention's "Last verified" line document?
options: The SQL Server version and date the script was last confirmed to still work correctly
The date the script was first written and never touched again
The name of whoever is currently on call
How many times the script has been run in production
questions.explain: DMV columns and behavior can change across SQL Server versions — "Last verified" tells the next person whether to trust the script or re-test it first.

questions.q: A script hardcodes WHERE name = 'AdventureWorks2019'. What's the fix to make it reusable?
options: Replace it with a DECLARE @DatabaseName sysname = NULL variable and a WHERE (@DatabaseName IS NULL OR name = @DatabaseName) clause
Delete the WHERE clause entirely so it always returns every row
Rename the database to something more generic
Nothing — hardcoding a database name is already a best practice
questions.explain: Declaring the database name as a parameter (defaulting to NULL for "all databases") is exactly the pattern this lesson demonstrates for turning a one-off query into a reusable script.
